newsitem.title: UK: Major speaks from heart with family values pledge.
newsitem.headline: Major speaks from heart with family values pledge.

text.p: John Major put family values at the top of the British election agenda on Wednesday with an initiative rooted in his own background as a child blighted by hard times but saved by a strong family.

The prime minister, whose father became an invalid while he was still a schoolboy, announced a 1.2 billion pound ($2 billion) plan of tax breaks for married men or women who gave up their jobs to care for their children or sick or handicapped relatives.
The initiative, announced in the ruling Conservative Party's manifesto for the May 1 election, was immediately challenged by the opposition parties who questioned how it would be funded.

But the surprise announcement allowed Major, way behind in opinion polls, to seize the initiative for the first time in the campaign and struck a chord in a nation concerned about the decline of the traditional family and the future of the young and vulnerable.

A spate of publicity about murders involving children, violent and unruly behaviour in schools and the collapse of one in three marriages in Britain has provoked a bout of soul-searching about what might have gone wrong in an otherwise prospering society.
Some seven million people now care for infirm relatives at home as an increasingly elderly population puts strain on health and social services.

Major's last foray into "family values" in 1993 backfired spectacularly when the media took it as a signal to root out skeletons in numerous MP's cupboards ranging from mistresses, illegitimate children and gay lovers.

But Major himself has one of the most stable and apparently happy family lives in British politics and made clear on Wednesday that he intended to support the dying institution of traditional marriage.

"We are in favour of marriage," he said. "Of course it (the tax proposal) helps strengthen the family, that's undoubtedly the case, and I very strongly welcome the fact. But it is a practical tax change to help people."
Conservative rightwingers see the increasing numbers of Britain women going to work as a factor in the rising divorce rate and lawlessness among children.
Norma Major, his wife of more than 20 years, stayed at home to bring up their two children while Major worked his way up from lowly bank clerk to member of parliament and, since 1990, prime minister.
As a child, Major saw poverty at first hand after his father lost his sight and his garden ornament business went bust, forcing the Majors to swop their home for a bleak apartment.
Major's sister Pat was later widowed at an early age and had to bring up her two young children alone.
His brother Terry said in an account of the times: "It was only the closeness of our relationship, fostered by our parents from early on, which kept us together in the long run."
Family action groups largely welcomed Major's attempts at social engineering.

"It is good news for families and marriage. We have been campaigning for three years specifically on this issue and how the tax system could get behind marriage," said Charlie Colchester of Christian Action Research and Education.
But the opposition Labour and Liberal Democrat parties were suspicious and Labour said the proposal would cost 5.2 billion pounds ($8 billion) if implemented in full, not 1.2 billion pounds.
